articles.title: Free Energy — The Criterion for Change
articles.description: Turning 'entropy of the universe increases' into something you can calculate for a system on a bench.
articles.intro: The second law says that spontaneous processes increase the total entropy of the universe. This is true, but not very useful. You would need to track the entropy of everything: system, atmosphere, bench, walls. Free energy solves this problem by folding the surroundings into a single quantity that depends only on the system.
body: Suppose you want to know whether a reaction will proceed spontaneously at constant temperature and pressure (the usual laboratory conditions). The second law requires $\Delta S_{\text{total}} \geq 0$, where:

You can measure $\Delta S_{\text{system}}$ from calorimetry. But $\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}$ is harder. The surroundings are large, and you did not set out to study them. However, if the process occurs at constant $T$ and $P$, the surroundings gain or lose entropy in a simple way: they absorb heat $-Q_P = -\Delta H_{\text{system}}$ at temperature $T$, so:
Substituting into the total entropy condition:
Multiply through by $-T$ (which flips the inequality):
The left-hand side is the change in a new quantity, the Gibbs free energy:
The criterion for spontaneous change at constant $T$ and $P$ is:

This is the single most important result in materials thermodynamics. A process at constant temperature and pressure is spontaneous if and only if it decreases the Gibbs free energy of the system. Equilibrium occurs when $G$ is at a minimum.

The Gibbs free energy lets you determine spontaneity by looking at the system alone. You never need to calculate the entropy of the surroundings explicitly. This is why $G$ appears everywhere in materials science: phase diagrams, reaction equilibria, electrochemistry, alloy design.
If the process occurs at constant $T$ and $V$ instead (less common in practice, but important in simulation and statistical mechanics), the analogous quantity is the Helmholtz free energy:
The spontaneity criterion becomes $\Delta F \leq 0$ at constant $T$ and $V$. The derivation is identical to the Gibbs case but starts from $dU$ rather than $dH$.

In materials science, most experimental work is at constant pressure, so Gibbs free energy dominates. In computational work (molecular dynamics, density functional theory), where the simulation cell has a fixed volume, Helmholtz free energy is more natural.
The competition between enthalpy and entropy
The expression $G = H - TS$ makes the competition explicit. A process can be spontaneous ($\Delta G < 0$) in two ways:
It can release energy ($\Delta H < 0$, exothermic) even if entropy decreases, provided the energy release is large enough.
It can increase entropy ($\Delta S > 0$) even if it costs energy, provided the entropy gain is large enough and the temperature is high enough.

The temperature acts as a dial that controls the balance. At low $T$, the $H$ term dominates: stable phases are those with strong bonds and low energy. At high $T$, the $TS$ term dominates: stable phases are those with high entropy and many accessible configurations.

This is why metals melt at high temperature (the liquid has higher entropy), why alloys disorder above a critical temperature (the disordered solid solution has higher configurational entropy), and why gaseous reactions become more favourable at high temperature if they produce more moles of gas.
G versus T: how to read a stability plot

Since $G = H - TS$, a plot of $G$ against $T$ at constant $P$ is a line with slope $-S$ (more precisely, $(\partial G / \partial T)_P = -S$). Phases with higher entropy have steeper downward slopes. The liquid always has a steeper slope than the solid because $S_{\text{liquid}} > S_{\text{solid}}$.

At low temperatures, the solid line sits below the liquid line: $G_{\text{solid}} < G_{\text{liquid}}$, so the solid is stable. As temperature increases, the steeper liquid line catches up. At the melting point $T_m$, the two lines cross: $G_{\text{solid}} = G_{\text{liquid}}$, and the two phases coexist in equilibrium. Above $T_m$, the liquid line is lower, and the liquid is stable.

For aluminium: $\Delta H_{\text{fus}} = 10.7$ kJ/mol and $\Delta S_{\text{fus}} = 11.5$ J/(mol$\cdot$K). At the melting point, $\Delta G_{\text{fus}} = \Delta H - T_m \Delta S = 0$, which gives $T_m = \Delta H / \Delta S = 10700 / 11.5 = 931$ K, close to the measured 933 K. The small discrepancy reflects the temperature dependence of $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ (Kirchhoff's law, article 5.3).

At 900 K (below $T_m$): $\Delta G_{\text{fus}} = 10700 - 900 \times 11.5 = +350$ J/mol. Positive: melting is not spontaneous. The solid is stable. At 1000 K (above $T_m$): $\Delta G_{\text{fus}} = 10700 - 1000 \times 11.5 = -800$ J/mol. Negative: melting is spontaneous. The liquid is stable. The numbers are small (hundreds of J/mol), which is why undercooling and superheating are possible in practice: the driving force near $T_m$ is weak.
For a chemical reaction, the standard Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^\circ$ is related to the equilibrium constant $K$ by:
A large negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means a large $K$: the reaction strongly favours products at equilibrium. A positive $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K < 1$: the reaction favours reactants.
For a general reaction at temperature $T$, the actual free energy change depends on the activities of reactants and products:
where $Q$ is the reaction quotient. At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K$, giving:

This equation is the bridge between thermodynamic tables (which give you $\Delta G^\circ$) and practical chemistry (which asks: what are the equilibrium concentrations?). We will use it extensively in the articles on Ellingham diagrams and predominance diagrams.

The standard free energy of formation of water vapour at 298 K is $\Delta G_f^\circ = -228.6$ kJ/mol. Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction 2H$_2$(g) + O$_2$(g) $\to$ 2H$_2$O(g) at 298 K. Comment on the result.

$K \approx 10^{80}$. This is an astronomically large number: the reaction overwhelmingly favours products at equilibrium. Thermodynamics says hydrogen and oxygen should react completely. The fact that a H$_2$/O$_2$ mixture can sit indefinitely at room temperature without reacting is entirely a kinetic effect (the activation energy is high). A spark provides the activation energy, and the reaction proceeds explosively.

articles.title: Chemical Potential — What Atoms Want
articles.description: Why atoms move from here to there, and the condition that makes them stop.
articles.intro: Temperature tells you which direction heat flows: from high T to low T. Pressure tells you which direction material flows in a fluid: from high P to low P. Chemical potential is the analogous quantity for the flow of atoms or molecules between phases, between regions, or between chemical species. It is the single most important concept in the thermodynamics of mixtures.
body: In a pure substance, every mole is identical. The molar Gibbs free energy is simply $G_m = G / n$. In a mixture, this is no longer true. Adding one mole of ethanol to a litre of water changes the free energy of the mixture by a different amount than adding one mole of ethanol to a litre of ethanol. The contribution of each component depends on the composition.
The partial molar Gibbs free energy of component $i$ in a mixture is:

This is the chemical potential of species $i$. It tells you how much the total free energy of the mixture changes when you add an infinitesimal amount of $i$, holding everything else constant. It depends on temperature, pressure, and composition.

The concept of partial molar quantities applies to any extensive property, not just $G$. The partial molar volume $\bar{V}_i = (\partial V / \partial n_i)_{T,P,n_j}$ tells you how the total volume changes when you add a mole of $i$. For an ideal solution, partial molar volumes equal the pure component values. For real solutions, they differ, sometimes significantly. Ethanol and water, for example, have a negative excess volume: mixing 50 mL of ethanol with 50 mL of water gives about 96 mL, not 100, because the molecules pack more efficiently together than apart.

Chemical potential is to mass transfer what temperature is to heat transfer. Atoms move spontaneously from regions of high $\mu$ to regions of low $\mu$, just as heat flows from high $T$ to low $T$. The system reaches equilibrium when $\mu_i$ is the same everywhere for every species.
This is the condition for chemical equilibrium in a mixture:

for every component $i$ across all phases $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots$. If $\mu_{\text{Cu}}$ is higher in the $\alpha$ phase than in the $\beta$ phase, copper atoms will diffuse from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ until the chemical potentials equalise. This is the thermodynamic driving force for diffusion, for phase transformations, and for chemical reactions.
Chemical potential of an ideal gas
For a pure ideal gas, the molar Gibbs free energy depends on pressure:
where $G_m^\circ$ is the value at the standard pressure $P^\circ = 1$ bar and $T$ is fixed. The logarithmic dependence on pressure comes from integrating $dG = V dP$ for an ideal gas ($V = RT/P$).
The pressure dependence of $G$ follows from the fundamental relation $dG = VdP - SdT$. At constant $T$:
For an ideal gas mixture, each component behaves as if it alone occupies the volume at its own partial pressure $p_i = x_i P$. The chemical potential of component $i$ is:

This is the starting point for all gas-phase equilibrium calculations. The chemical potential increases with partial pressure: a gas at high pressure has higher $\mu$ than the same gas at low pressure, which is why gases expand spontaneously from high to low pressure.
For solids and liquids, the pressure dependence of $\mu$ is much weaker (because $V_m$ is small), and the composition dependence dominates. For an ideal solution:

where $\mu_i^*$ is the chemical potential of pure $i$ at the same $T$ and $P$, and $x_i$ is its mole fraction. Since $x_i < 1$, $\ln x_i < 0$, and $\mu_i < \mu_i^*$. Dissolving a substance in a mixture always lowers its chemical potential relative to the pure state. This is the fundamental thermodynamic reason why mixing tends to happen spontaneously.
For real (non-ideal) solutions, the mole fraction is replaced by the activity $a_i$, which we will define in the next article:
The chemical potentials of all components in a mixture are linked by the Gibbs-Duhem equation:
At constant $T$ and $P$, this reduces to:
If you increase the chemical potential of one component, the chemical potentials of the others must decrease to compensate. For a binary system ($i$ = A, B):

This is a powerful consistency check. If you measure or model $\mu_A$ as a function of composition, the Gibbs-Duhem equation fixes $\mu_B$. You cannot choose both independently. It also means that in practice, you only need to measure the activity of one component in a binary; the other is determined.
In a binary A-B ideal solution, show that $\mu_A$ decreases as $x_B$ increases. What is the physical interpretation?
For an ideal solution: $\mu_A = \mu_A^* + RT \ln x_A = \mu_A^* + RT \ln(1 - x_B)$.
Since $0 < x_B < 1$, we have $0 < (1 - x_B) < 1$, so $\ln(1 - x_B) < 0$, and $\mu_A < \mu_A^*$. As $x_B$ increases, $x_A$ decreases, $\ln x_A$ becomes more negative, and $\mu_A$ drops.

Physically: diluting A reduces its chemical potential. A atoms in a mixture are more "content" (lower $\mu$) than in the pure state, because the mixture has higher configurational entropy. This is why mixing tends to be spontaneous. It is also why boiling points are elevated and freezing points are depressed in solutions: the lower $\mu$ of the solvent stabilises the liquid phase.

articles.title: Activity & Real Behaviour
articles.description: Raoult's law, Henry's law, activity coefficients, and standard states — handling non-ideal reality.
articles.intro: In an ideal solution, the chemical potential of each component depends only on its mole fraction. Real solutions are not ideal. Atoms interact with each other, and those interactions change the thermodynamics. Activity is the quantity that accounts for this.
body: Why mole fraction is not enough

The ideal solution expression $\mu_i = \mu_i^* + RT \ln x_i$ assumes that an atom of species A does not care whether its neighbours are A atoms or B atoms. The energy of mixing is zero, and the only driving force for mixing is the configurational entropy gain. This is a reasonable approximation for some systems (Ge-Si, for example, where the atoms are almost the same size and have similar bonding), but it is badly wrong for most.

In a Cu-Ni alloy, copper and nickel atoms have different sizes and different electronic structures. Their interactions are not the same as Cu-Cu or Ni-Ni interactions. The enthalpy of mixing is nonzero, and the chemical potential depends on composition in a more complicated way than $RT \ln x_i$.
Activity is the fix. We define the activity $a_i$ of component $i$ so that the chemical potential always takes the same mathematical form:
For an ideal solution, $a_i = x_i$. For a real solution, $a_i \neq x_i$, and the ratio defines the activity coefficient:

The activity coefficient $\gamma_i$ captures all the non-ideal behaviour. If $\gamma_i > 1$, the component is more "eager" to escape the solution than ideal mixing would predict (positive deviation). If $\gamma_i < 1$, it is less eager (negative deviation). If $\gamma_i = 1$, the solution is ideal with respect to that component at that composition.

In the limit where $x_i \to 1$ (nearly pure $i$), the environment around an $i$ atom is almost entirely other $i$ atoms. The solution behaves ideally from $i$'s perspective, and $\gamma_i \to 1$. This limit is Raoult's law:

Raoult's law is exact in the limit of a dilute solute in a solvent, from the solvent's point of view. If you dissolve a trace of tin in liquid copper, the activity of copper is essentially equal to its mole fraction. The copper atoms barely notice the tin.

In the opposite limit, $x_i \to 0$ (trace amounts of $i$), every $i$ atom is surrounded entirely by the other component. The environment is consistent but different from pure $i$. In this limit, $\gamma_i$ approaches a constant value $\gamma_i^\circ \neq 1$, and:

This is Henry's law. The activity is proportional to $x_i$ but with a different proportionality constant. Henry's law constant $\gamma_i^\circ$ (or equivalently $k_H = \gamma_i^\circ P_i^*$ for gas solubility) is a measurable property of the dilute solution.

Henry's law is the foundation of dilute solution thermodynamics. In metallurgy, dissolved oxygen in liquid iron, nitrogen in liquid steel, and hydrogen in titanium all obey Henry's law at low concentrations. The Sievert's law for gas dissolution ($C \propto \sqrt{P}$) is a consequence of Henry's law applied to diatomic gases that dissociate on dissolving.
The choice of standard state determines the numerical value of $a_i$. There are two common conventions:

Raoultian standard state: pure component $i$ at the same $T$ and $P$. Then $\mu_i^\circ = \mu_i^*$, $a_i = \gamma_i x_i$, and $\gamma_i \to 1$ as $x_i \to 1$. This is the standard choice for components present in large amounts (solvents, major alloying elements).

Henrian standard state: the hypothetical state of pure $i$ obeying Henry's law. Then $\gamma_i \to 1$ as $x_i \to 0$, and activity equals mole fraction in the dilute limit. This is the natural choice for trace solutes (dissolved gases, impurities).

The two conventions assign different numerical values to $a_i$ for the same physical state, because they use different reference points. The chemical potential $\mu_i$ itself is the same regardless of convention; only the split between $\mu_i^\circ$ and $RT \ln a_i$ changes. Confusion about standard states is one of the most common sources of error in applied thermodynamics. Always check which convention a database or textbook is using.
Activities can be measured in several ways:

From vapour pressure: $a_i = p_i / p_i^*$, where $p_i$ is the partial pressure over the solution and $p_i^*$ is the vapour pressure of pure $i$ at the same temperature. This works well for volatile components.
From electrochemical measurements: an electrochemical cell with electrodes in the solution and in the pure component gives an EMF directly related to $\ln a_i$ through the Nernst equation.

From phase equilibrium: if two phases coexist, the equality of chemical potentials ($\mu_i^\alpha = \mu_i^\beta$) constrains the activities. Liquidus measurements in binary phase diagrams are essentially activity measurements.
From calorimetry: measuring the enthalpy of mixing gives $H^{\text{excess}}$, from which activity coefficients can be derived via the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation.

In practice, the CALPHAD method uses all of these data sources simultaneously, fitting model parameters to reproduce measured phase diagrams, enthalpies, and activities across entire composition and temperature ranges.

In liquid Fe-Ni alloys at 1600°C, the activity coefficient of Ni follows approximately $\ln \gamma_{\text{Ni}} = -1.3(1 - x_{\text{Ni}})^2$ (Raoultian standard state). Calculate the activity of Ni in an alloy with $x_{\text{Ni}} = 0.3$.

The activity (0.159) is about half the mole fraction (0.3). This is a negative deviation: $\gamma < 1$, meaning Fe-Ni interactions are more favourable than Ni-Ni interactions. Ni is more stable in the iron solution than ideal mixing would predict. This is consistent with the strong compound-forming tendency of the Fe-Ni system (FeNi$_3$ is an ordered phase).

articles.title: Solutions & Mixing
articles.description: What happens when you put two things together — ideal solutions, excess properties, and the meaning of mixing quantities.
articles.intro: When two pure substances are combined into a single phase, every thermodynamic property changes. The free energy of the mixture is not simply the sum of the free energies of the pure components. Understanding exactly how and why it differs is the foundation of alloy thermodynamics.
body: For any extensive property $Y$ (free energy, enthalpy, entropy, volume), the mixing quantity $\Delta Y_{\text{mix}}$ is the difference between the value in the solution and the weighted sum of the pure component values:
where $Y_i^*$ is the molar value for pure $i$. The mixing quantity tells you what changes when you form the solution. For the Gibbs free energy of a binary A-B solution:

If $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} < 0$, the solution is more stable than the unmixed pure components, and mixing is spontaneous. If $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} > 0$ at some composition, the system prefers to separate into two phases at that composition.

The ideal solution is the simplest model. It assumes that A-B interactions are identical to A-A and B-B interactions: the atoms do not care what their neighbours are. The only change on mixing is configurational entropy.
The mixing quantities for an ideal solution are:
\Delta G_{\text{mix}}^{\text{ideal}} = RT \left[ x_A \ln x_A + x_B \ln x_B \right]

The entropy of mixing is always positive (since $\ln x < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$), so the free energy of mixing is always negative. An ideal solution is stable at all compositions and all temperatures. It never phase-separates.

At 1000 K and $x_A = x_B = 0.5$: $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}^{\text{ideal}} = 1000 \times 8.314 \times (0.5 \ln 0.5 + 0.5 \ln 0.5) = -5.76$ kJ/mol. That is a significant stabilisation. Even weak chemical interactions have to overcome this entropic driving force to cause phase separation.
Real solutions differ from ideal ones. The difference is captured by excess properties:

The excess free energy $G^{\text{excess}}$ is the part of the mixing free energy that is not accounted for by ideal configurational entropy. It contains all the information about the actual atomic interactions.
G^{\text{excess}} = \Delta G_{\text{mix}} - RT \left[ x_A \ln x_A + x_B \ln x_B \right]
The excess free energy is related to the activity coefficients:

If $G^{\text{excess}} < 0$, A-B interactions are more favourable than the average of A-A and B-B: the solution is more stable than ideal (negative deviation, $\gamma < 1$). If $G^{\text{excess}} > 0$, A-B interactions are less favourable: the solution is less stable than ideal (positive deviation, $\gamma > 1$), and at high enough $G^{\text{excess}}$ the system may phase-separate.

The excess free energy can be decomposed: $G^{\text{excess}} = H^{\text{excess}} - T S^{\text{excess}}$. The excess enthalpy $H^{\text{excess}} = \Delta H_{\text{mix}}$ (since the ideal enthalpy of mixing is zero). The excess entropy $S^{\text{excess}}$ accounts for non-random arrangements (short-range order or clustering).
Some real numbers for liquid alloys at approximately equimolar composition near their liquidus:
Cu-Ni: $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} \approx +2$ kJ/mol (slightly endothermic, atoms weakly repel)
Cu-Zn: $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} \approx -8$ kJ/mol (exothermic, strong compound-forming tendency)
Au-Si: $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} \approx -15$ kJ/mol (very exothermic, deep eutectic)

The sign and magnitude of $\Delta H_{\text{mix}}$ determine the shape of the phase diagram. Strongly negative mixing enthalpies produce compound-forming systems with high melting intermediates. Positive mixing enthalpies produce miscibility gaps. Near-zero values produce simple lens-shaped diagrams with complete solid solubility.

Given a curve of $G_{\text{mix}}$ versus composition, the chemical potentials of A and B at any composition $x_B$ are found by drawing the tangent to the curve at that point. The intercepts of the tangent with the $x_B = 0$ and $x_B = 1$ axes give $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ respectively.

This geometric construction is not just a mathematical trick. It is how phase equilibrium is determined graphically. When two phases coexist (say, solid and liquid), the tangent lines to their respective $G(x)$ curves must be the same line (the common tangent). The points of tangency give the equilibrium compositions of the two phases. We will use this construction extensively in article 5.15.

The thermodynamics of mixing is the foundation of everything that follows in this module. The regular solution model (article 5.13) gives $G^{\text{excess}}$ a simple functional form that captures the essential physics. The common tangent construction (article 5.15) turns $G(x)$ curves into phase diagrams. Ellingham diagrams (article 5.16) are just $\Delta G^\circ$ versus $T$ for oxidation reactions. Every applied tool in materials thermodynamics rests on the concepts of mixing free energy, excess properties, and chemical potential.
Calculate $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ for an ideal binary solution at $x_B = 0.3$ and $T = 1200$ K. Compare this to the thermal energy $RT$.

$RT = 9977$ J/mol. So $|\Delta G_{\text{mix}}| \approx 0.61 \times RT$. The entropic driving force for mixing is a substantial fraction of the thermal energy scale. An enthalpy of mixing would need to exceed about 6 kJ/mol (positive) to overcome this and cause phase separation at this temperature.

articles.title: The Regular Solution Model
articles.description: The simplest model that captures real alloy behaviour — and a slider that builds a phase diagram.
articles.intro: The ideal solution assumes atoms are indifferent to their neighbours. Real atoms are not. The regular solution model adds one parameter to capture this: an interaction energy that makes mixing either favourable or unfavourable. With that single parameter, the model predicts miscibility gaps, critical temperatures, and the onset of spinodal decomposition.
body: The regular solution model assumes that the excess enthalpy of mixing is proportional to $x_A x_B$:

where $\Omega$ is the interaction parameter, with units of J/mol. The excess entropy is assumed to be zero: atoms are randomly distributed on the lattice regardless of their interactions. This is the "regular" assumption: the enthalpy is non-ideal but the entropy is still ideal.
The total free energy of mixing is then:
\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = \Omega \, x_A x_B + RT \left[ x_A \ln x_A + x_B \ln x_B \right]
The first term is the enthalpy of mixing (the interaction energy). The second is the ideal entropy contribution. The balance between them determines whether the solution is stable.

The interaction parameter can be related to nearest-neighbour bond energies. If $\varepsilon_{AA}$, $\varepsilon_{BB}$ and $\varepsilon_{AB}$ are the bond energies for each type of pair, and $z$ is the coordination number, then:

If A-B bonds are weaker than the average of A-A and B-B bonds, $\Omega > 0$ (endothermic mixing, atoms prefer their own kind). If A-B bonds are stronger, $\Omega < 0$ (exothermic mixing, compound-forming tendency).

Typical values: Cu-Ni has $\Omega \approx +12$ kJ/mol (mild positive, miscibility gap at low temperature). Au-Ni has $\Omega \approx +30$ kJ/mol (strong positive, wide miscibility gap). Cu-Zn has $\Omega \approx -30$ kJ/mol (strong negative, ordered compounds form).
When $\Omega = 0$, the $G_{\text{mix}}$ curve is the familiar ideal-mixing parabola, concave up everywhere. The solution is stable at all compositions.

When $\Omega > 0$, the positive enthalpy term pushes the centre of the curve upward. At low temperature (where the $TS$ term is weak), the curve develops two minima and a central hump: it becomes concave down in the middle and concave up at the edges. The solution is unstable at intermediate compositions and wants to separate into an A-rich phase and a B-rich phase.
The critical condition is found by setting $\partial^2 \Delta G_{\text{mix}} / \partial x^2 = 0$ at $x = 0.5$:
The critical temperature for a symmetric miscibility gap is $T_c = \Omega / 2R$. Below this temperature, the solution separates. Above it, entropy wins and the solution is stable.
At $x_B = 0.5$, the second derivative of $\Delta G_{\text{mix}}$ with respect to $x_B$ is:

For Cu-Ni ($\Omega \approx 12$ kJ/mol): $T_c = 12000 / (2 \times 8.314) \approx 720$ K. The experimental miscibility gap closes at about 630 K. The regular solution model overestimates somewhat (it neglects short-range order and the temperature dependence of $\Omega$), but it captures the physics correctly.

Within the miscibility gap, there are two regimes. Between the spinodal points (where $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 = 0$), the free energy curve is concave down. Any infinitesimal fluctuation in composition lowers the free energy, so decomposition proceeds spontaneously without nucleation. This is spinodal decomposition.

Between the spinodal and the binodal (the equilibrium phase boundary), the curve is concave up but the system is still metastable: it can lower its energy by decomposing, but it needs a finite composition fluctuation (a nucleus) to get over the energy barrier. This is nucleation and growth.

The distinction matters for microstructure. Spinodal decomposition produces a fine, interconnected two-phase structure with a characteristic wavelength. Nucleation and growth produces discrete precipitates in a matrix. Both are predicted by the shape of the $G(x)$ curve, which the regular solution model gives explicitly.

The regular solution model is symmetric: the $G_{\text{mix}}$ curve is the same for $x_A$ and $x_B$. Real systems are rarely symmetric. The model also uses a single, composition-independent $\Omega$, which is a significant simplification.
The CALPHAD approach extends this by writing $G^{\text{excess}}$ as a Redlich-Kister polynomial:

The $L_0$ term is the regular solution. Higher-order terms ($L_1, L_2, \ldots$) add asymmetry and composition dependence. These parameters are fitted to experimental data (phase boundaries, enthalpies of mixing, activity measurements) and stored in thermodynamic databases used by software like Thermo-Calc, FactSage, and Pandat. The regular solution model is the conceptual core of all of these tools.
A binary alloy has $\Omega = 20$ kJ/mol. Calculate the critical temperature $T_c$ for the miscibility gap. At 800 K, is the equimolar alloy stable as a single phase or does it phase-separate?
At 800 K ($T/T_c = 0.665$), we are below $T_c$, so the equimolar alloy is inside the miscibility gap and will phase-separate into an A-rich and a B-rich phase.

The second derivative is negative: the free energy curve is concave down at $x = 0.5$. The alloy is not just metastable but actually inside the spinodal. It will decompose spontaneously without needing nucleation.

articles.title: Phase Equilibria & the Gibbs Phase Rule
articles.description: How many phases can coexist, and what fixes what.
articles.intro: A binary eutectic system can have liquid, solid A, and solid B all present simultaneously, but only at one specific temperature and composition. A pure substance can exist as solid, liquid, and gas together only at a single point in the PT diagram. These are not coincidences. The Gibbs phase rule tells you exactly how many variables you are free to choose when multiple phases coexist.
body: Phases, components, and degrees of freedom

A phase is a physically distinct, homogeneous region of matter. Liquid water is one phase. Ice is another. Steam is a third. In a Cu-Zn alloy, the $\alpha$ (FCC) solid solution is one phase, the $\beta$ (BCC) phase is another, and the liquid is a third. Each phase has its own composition, structure, and properties.

A component is the minimum number of independent chemical species needed to describe the composition of every phase. For a Cu-Zn alloy, you need two components (Cu and Zn). For the water system, you need one (H₂O, since hydrogen and oxygen are always in 2:1 ratio). For a system where CaO and SiO₂ react to form CaSiO₃, you need two components (CaO and SiO₂), not three, because the compound's composition is determined by the other two.
The degrees of freedom $F$ (or variance) is the number of intensive variables you can independently change without changing the number of phases present.
where $C$ is the number of components, $P$ is the number of phases, and the 2 accounts for temperature and pressure.

The phase rule follows from counting equations and unknowns. Each phase in a $C$-component system is described by $C - 1$ independent composition variables plus $T$ and $P$, giving $P(C - 1) + 2$ total variables. The equilibrium conditions ($\mu_i^\alpha = \mu_i^\beta$ for each component between each pair of phases) provide $(P - 1)C$ equations. The degrees of freedom are the difference: $F = P(C-1) + 2 - (P-1)C = C - P + 2$.
Variables: each phase has $C - 1$ independent mole fractions, plus $T$ and $P$ shared by all phases. Total: $P(C-1) + 2$.
Constraints: for each of $C$ components, the chemical potential must be equal across all $P$ phases. That gives $(P-1)$ independent equations per component, so $(P-1)C$ total.
What the phase rule tells you
One phase ($P = 1$): $F = 2$. You can vary both $T$ and $P$ freely. This is a region in the PT diagram.
Two phases ($P = 2$): $F = 1$. Fix $T$ and $P$ is determined (or vice versa). This is a line in the PT diagram (the melting curve, the boiling curve).
Three phases ($P = 3$): $F = 0$. No freedom at all. This is a single point: the triple point. For water, 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa.
You cannot have four phases in equilibrium for a one-component system. $F$ would be $-1$, which is meaningless. The phase rule forbids it.
One phase: $F = 3$ ($T$, $P$, and composition). If pressure is fixed (as it usually is in metallurgy), $F = 2$: the familiar single-phase regions in a binary phase diagram.

Two phases: $F = 2$ at variable pressure, $F = 1$ at fixed pressure. On a temperature-composition diagram at 1 atm, two-phase regions are areas (not lines), but within them, specifying $T$ fixes both phase compositions.
Three phases: $F = 1$ at variable pressure, $F = 0$ at fixed pressure. This is a horizontal line on the phase diagram: a eutectic, peritectic, or eutectoid reaction at a single temperature.

The phase rule does not tell you which phases are present or what their compositions are. It only tells you how many independent variables you have once you know the number of phases. The actual phase diagram must be determined experimentally or calculated from free energy models.

The phase rule applies to true equilibrium. In practice, systems often fail to reach equilibrium. A supersaturated solid solution is a single phase with $F = 2$ (at fixed $P$), but it is not the equilibrium state. The phase rule correctly describes the metastable state (one phase, two degrees of freedom) but does not tell you that the system "should" decompose into two phases. Recognising the difference between stable and metastable equilibria is one of the key skills in applied materials thermodynamics.

In the Fe-C binary phase diagram at 1 atm, the eutectoid reaction occurs at 727°C: austenite ($\gamma$) $\to$ ferrite ($\alpha$) + cementite (Fe$_3$C). How many degrees of freedom does the system have at the eutectoid point?
$C = 2$ (Fe and C), $P = 3$ ($\gamma$, $\alpha$, Fe$_3$C). At fixed pressure:

Zero degrees of freedom. The temperature (727°C) and the compositions of all three phases are completely fixed. You cannot change any variable without losing one of the three phases. This is why the eutectoid appears as a single horizontal line on the phase diagram, not as a region.

articles.title: From Free Energy to Phase Diagrams
articles.description: G-x curves, the common tangent construction, and how binary phase diagrams emerge from thermodynamics.
articles.intro: A phase diagram is a map of stability. At each temperature and composition, it tells you which phases are present at equilibrium. This article shows where that map comes from: a set of free energy curves, one for each phase, evaluated at each temperature. The common tangent construction converts these curves into the familiar boundaries of a phase diagram.
body: Consider a binary A-B system with two possible phases: liquid (L) and solid ($\alpha$). At a given temperature, each phase has its own Gibbs free energy as a function of composition:
G^L(x_B) = x_A G_A^{*,L} + x_B G_B^{*,L} + \Delta G_{\text{mix}}^L(x_B)
G^\alpha(x_B) = x_A G_A^{*,\alpha} + x_B G_B^{*,\alpha} + \Delta G_{\text{mix}}^\alpha(x_B)
where $G_i^{*,\phi}$ is the free energy of pure $i$ in phase $\phi$. These are different for solid and liquid: $G_A^{*,L} \neq G_A^{*,\alpha}$ unless $T$ is exactly the melting point of pure A.

At a temperature above the melting points of both components, $G^L < G^\alpha$ at all compositions: the liquid curve sits entirely below the solid curve, and the system is liquid everywhere. At a temperature below the melting points of both, the solid curve sits below the liquid. At intermediate temperatures, the curves cross, and both phases are stable over different composition ranges.

When two free energy curves overlap in composition space, the equilibrium state is found by the common tangent construction. Draw the line that is tangent to both curves simultaneously. The compositions at the two points of tangency are the equilibrium compositions of the two phases.

Why does this work? At equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component must be the same in both phases: $\mu_A^L = \mu_A^\alpha$ and $\mu_B^L = \mu_B^\alpha$. Recall from article 5.12 that the chemical potentials are given by the intercepts of the tangent to the $G(x)$ curve. If the tangent line is the same for both curves, both intercepts match, and both chemical potential conditions are satisfied simultaneously.
The region between the two tangent compositions is a two-phase region. At any overall composition in this range, the system separates into the two equilibrium phases.

If the overall composition $x_0$ falls in a two-phase region at temperature $T$, the system splits into two phases with compositions given by the phase boundaries (the tie line endpoints). The lever rule tells you how much of each phase is present.
Conservation of mass requires that the total amount of B in the system equals the sum of B in each phase:
where $f^L$ and $f^S = 1 - f^L$ are the mole fractions of liquid and solid. Solving:
f^L = \frac{x_B^S - x_0}{x_B^S - x_B^L} \qquad f^S = \frac{x_0 - x_B^L}{x_B^S - x_B^L}

The name comes from the analogy to a mechanical lever. Think of the tie line as a beam balanced at the overall composition. The "weight" of each phase is proportional to the length of the beam on the opposite side. An overall composition close to the solidus gives mostly solid. Close to the liquidus gives mostly liquid.

A Cu-Ni alloy with overall composition $x_{\text{Ni}} = 0.50$ at 1500 K. From the phase diagram, the liquidus is at $x_{\text{Ni}}^L = 0.38$ and the solidus at $x_{\text{Ni}}^S = 0.58$. The fraction of solid is $f^S = (0.50 - 0.38) / (0.58 - 0.38) = 0.60$. The alloy is 60% solid, 40% liquid. The solid is Ni-rich (0.58); the liquid is Cu-rich (0.38).
Drag the point on the diagram below into the two-phase region to see the tie line and phase fractions update live:
Building a phase diagram temperature by temperature

Repeat the common tangent construction at many temperatures. At each temperature, you get a pair of equilibrium compositions (or none, if one curve sits entirely below the other). Plot these compositions against temperature and you have a phase diagram.
For a simple lens-shaped system (complete solid solubility, e.g. Cu-Ni at high temperature):
Above the melting point of both components: liquid everywhere. Single-phase liquid region.

At high temperature: the liquid curve is lower than the solid over most of the composition range, but the solid curve is starting to come down on the component with the highest melting point. The common tangent touches near the pure-B side. A narrow two-phase (L + $\alpha$) region appears.
At intermediate temperature: the two curves overlap more, the common tangent touches further from the edges, and the two-phase region widens.
Below the melting point of both: the solid curve sits entirely below the liquid. Single-phase solid.
The upper boundary of the two-phase region (the locus of liquid compositions) is the liquidus. The lower boundary (the locus of solid compositions) is the solidus.

If the solid phase has a positive mixing enthalpy ($\Omega > 0$ for the solid), the solid $G(x)$ curve develops a hump at intermediate compositions, while the liquid curve (with its weaker interactions) remains smoothly concave. At some temperature, the common tangent from the A-rich solid to the B-rich solid passes through the liquid curve. Below this temperature, it is more favourable to form a mixture of two solids than a single solid solution.

The temperature at which three phases (liquid, $\alpha$, $\beta$) coexist is the eutectic temperature. The composition at which the liquid transforms directly into the two-solid mixture is the eutectic composition. On the phase diagram, this appears as a horizontal line connecting the three-phase compositions (a eutectic isotherm), with a V-shaped liquidus above it.

The Pb-Sn system is a classic eutectic. Lead and tin have limited solid solubility (positive $\Omega$ in the solid). The eutectic is at 183°C and 61.9 wt% Sn. Below 183°C, the system consists of Pb-rich $\alpha$ and Sn-rich $\beta$. This is the basis of traditional solder.

The same logic extends to any number of phases. Add an intermediate compound (an ordered phase with its own $G(x)$ curve, typically with a deep minimum at its stoichiometric composition), and you get peritectic reactions and additional two-phase regions. Add a gas phase, and you can construct oxide stability diagrams.

In every case, the procedure is the same: write down $G(x)$ for each phase at each temperature, find the common tangents, and plot the tangent compositions against temperature. This is exactly what CALPHAD software does, using optimised Gibbs energy models for each phase, fitted to experimental data.

The conceptual point: a phase diagram is not a separate piece of information from the free energy curves. It is a different way of presenting the same information. If you understand $G(x)$ curves and the common tangent, you can read any phase diagram, predict the effect of changing temperature or composition, and understand why the boundaries are where they are.

In a Cu-Ni alloy at 1500 K, the liquidus composition is $x_{\text{Ni}}^L = 0.38$ and the solidus is $x_{\text{Ni}}^S = 0.58$. An alloy with overall composition $x_{\text{Ni}} = 0.45$ is cooled slowly through this temperature. What phases are present, what are their compositions, and what fraction of the alloy is solid?

At 1500 K, $x_0 = 0.45$ lies between $x^L = 0.38$ and $x^S = 0.58$. The alloy is in the two-phase (L + S) region. The liquid has composition $x_{\text{Ni}} = 0.38$ and the solid has composition $x_{\text{Ni}} = 0.58$.

The alloy is 35% solid and 65% liquid. The solid is Ni-enriched relative to the overall composition; the liquid is Cu-enriched. As cooling continues, both compositions shift along the solidus and liquidus curves, and the fraction of solid increases until the last liquid disappears at the solidus temperature for $x_0 = 0.45$.

articles.title: Ellingham Diagrams
articles.description: Which oxides are stable? Reading these charts like a metallurgist.
articles.intro: If you heat a metal in air, will it oxidise? If so, can you reduce the oxide back to the metal using carbon? At what temperature? The Ellingham diagram answers all of these questions on a single chart. It is one of the most practically useful constructions in materials thermodynamics.
body: Consider the oxidation of a metal M:

The standard Gibbs free energy change for this reaction, $\Delta G^\circ$, tells you whether the oxide is stable at a given temperature. If $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, the oxide is thermodynamically favoured over the metal in the presence of oxygen at 1 atm. If $\Delta G^\circ > 0$, the metal is stable and the oxide will decompose.

An Ellingham diagram plots $\Delta G^\circ$ for the formation of various oxides against temperature, all normalised to consume one mole of O₂. By plotting all reactions on the same basis, you can compare them directly.
Each line on the Ellingham diagram represents one oxidation reaction. The lines are approximately straight because:

and both $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are roughly constant with temperature (Kirchhoff corrections are small for most oxide reactions). The slope of each line is $-\Delta S^\circ$. Since the oxidation reaction consumes one mole of gas (O₂), $\Delta S^\circ$ is negative (loss of gas-phase entropy), and the lines slope upward. The more negative $\Delta S^\circ$ (more gas consumed), the steeper the upward slope.

Kinks in the lines occur at phase transitions of the metal or oxide. Melting increases the entropy of the metal, making $\Delta S^\circ$ more negative (the solid-to-liquid transition adds entropy to the reactant side), so the line becomes steeper. Boiling of the metal makes an even larger change.

The lower a line sits on the diagram, the more negative $\Delta G^\circ$ and the more stable the oxide. The oxides of calcium, magnesium and aluminium sit near the bottom: they are very stable and very difficult to reduce. The oxides of copper, nickel and iron sit higher: they are less stable and easier to reduce.
If metal A has a lower (more negative) $\Delta G^\circ$ line than metal B, then A can reduce the oxide of B. Aluminium sits below iron on the Ellingham diagram, so aluminium can reduce iron oxide:

This is the thermite reaction. It is violently exothermic because the difference in $\Delta G^\circ$ between Al₂O₃ and Fe₂O₃ is large (about $-800$ kJ per mole of O₂ at room temperature). The further apart two lines are on the Ellingham diagram, the larger the driving force for the reduction reaction.
Carbon is the most important reducing agent in metallurgy. It appears on the Ellingham diagram as two reactions:

The CO₂ line is almost horizontal because one mole of gas is consumed and one is produced ($\Delta S^\circ \approx 0$). The CO line slopes downward because one mole of gas is consumed but two are produced ($\Delta S^\circ > 0$, positive, unlike most oxidation reactions). The two lines cross at about 700°C.

Below 700°C, the CO₂ reaction is more favourable and carbon reduces oxides that sit above the CO₂ line. Above 700°C, the CO reaction takes over and carbon can reduce progressively more stable oxides as temperature increases. This is why smelting furnaces operate at high temperatures: the reducing power of carbon increases with temperature.

Iron oxide sits above the carbon lines above about 700°C, which is why iron smelting in a blast furnace works. Aluminium oxide sits below the carbon lines at all temperatures, which is why aluminium cannot be smelted from its ore using carbon. It must be reduced electrolytically (the Hall-Héroult process).

The Ellingham diagram also gives the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure for each reaction. Since $\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K$ and for the reaction $2\text{M} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{MO}$, $K = 1/P_{\text{O}_2}$ (activities of pure solids are 1), we have:

At any point on an Ellingham line, you can read off the $P_{\text{O}_2}$ below which the metal is stable and above which the oxide is stable. For aluminium at 1000 K, $\Delta G^\circ \approx -1000$ kJ/mol O₂, giving $P_{\text{O}_2} \approx 10^{-52}$ atm. This is an absurdly small number. It means aluminium oxide is stable in any environment that contains even a trace of oxygen. For copper at 1000 K, $\Delta G^\circ \approx -200$ kJ, giving $P_{\text{O}_2} \approx 10^{-10}$ atm, which is achievable in a good vacuum or reducing atmosphere.

This is how metallurgists choose processing atmospheres. To prevent oxidation during heat treatment, you need $P_{\text{O}_2}$ below the equilibrium value. For steel, a forming gas (N₂/H₂ mix) suffices. For titanium, even ultra-high vacuum may not be enough, which is why titanium processing uses argon atmospheres and avoids any oxygen exposure.
The Ellingham line for aluminium oxidation is approximately $\Delta G^\circ = -1120 + 0.21T$ kJ per mol O$_2$. At 1000 K, what is the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure in atm?

This is an extraordinarily small number. Any detectable amount of oxygen will oxidise aluminium at 1000 K. Alumina is one of the most stable oxides, which is why aluminium is so difficult to produce from its ore and why the protective Al$_2$O$_3$ film on aluminium surfaces is so robust.

articles.title: Predominance Diagrams
articles.description: Pourbaix diagrams and stability domains — thermodynamics meets electrochemistry.
articles.intro: An Ellingham diagram maps oxide stability against temperature. A predominance diagram maps stability against two variables simultaneously: typically oxygen partial pressure and temperature, or electrode potential and pH. These are the thermodynamic maps that corrosion engineers, hydrometallurgists, and electrochemists use every day.
body: A predominance diagram (also called a stability area diagram or Kellogg diagram) plots the regions where different compounds of a metal are stable as a function of two environmental variables. The most common axes are $\log P_{\text{O}_2}$ versus $\log P_{\text{S}_2}$ (for roasting of sulphide ores) or $\log P_{\text{O}_2}$ versus temperature (for high-temperature oxidation).

Each boundary line on the diagram represents equilibrium between two adjacent phases. On one side of the line, one phase is stable; on the other side, the other is stable. The lines are calculated from the condition $\Delta G = 0$ for the reaction converting one phase to the other. Inside each region, one phase has the lowest free energy.

For the Cu-O-S system, the predominance diagram at a given temperature shows regions of Cu (metal), Cu₂O, CuO, Cu₂S, and CuSO₄. A roasting engineer uses this to choose the atmosphere (oxygen and sulphur pressures) that converts copper sulphide ore to metallic copper without forming unwanted copper sulphate.

The Pourbaix diagram (also called a potential-pH diagram) is the most widely used predominance diagram in materials science. It plots electrode potential $E$ against pH for a metal-water system at a fixed temperature (usually 25°C). The diagram shows which species (metal, oxide, hydroxide, dissolved ions) is thermodynamically stable at each combination of potential and pH.
The diagram contains three types of boundary:
Horizontal lines: pure electrochemical reactions (no H⁺ or OH⁻ involved). The equilibrium potential depends only on the activities of the metal species, not on pH.
Vertical lines: pure chemical reactions (no electron transfer). The equilibrium depends only on pH, not on potential. Dissolution of an oxide in acid, for example.
Sloping lines: reactions involving both electron transfer and H⁺/OH⁻. The slope is determined by the stoichiometry, following the Nernst equation.

The Pourbaix diagram for iron at 25°C is the most commonly cited example. At low pH and low potential, Fe²⁺ ions are stable: the iron dissolves as ferrous ions. This is active corrosion. At higher potential, Fe³⁺ becomes stable (ferric ions). At intermediate pH and higher potential, Fe₂O₃ (rust) or Fe₃O₄ (magnetite) form a stable solid on the surface. This is the passive region: the oxide film protects the metal from further corrosion. At high pH, soluble ferrate species can form, but these are rarely important in practice.

At the bottom of the diagram, at very negative potentials, metallic iron is stable regardless of pH. This is the immunity region: the metal is thermodynamically stable and does not corrode. Cathodic protection works by shifting the potential of a steel structure into this region (using sacrificial anodes or impressed current).
The diagram also shows two dashed lines representing the stability limits of water:
The upper dashed line: above this, water is oxidised to O₂. $E = 1.23 - 0.059 \times \text{pH}$ V at 25°C.
The lower dashed line: below this, water is reduced to H₂. $E = -0.059 \times \text{pH}$ V at 25°C.
These lines define the electrochemical window of water. Corrosion processes in aqueous environments must lie between them (unless the water itself is being electrolysed).
Pourbaix diagrams are thermodynamic constructions. They tell you what is stable, not what actually happens in practice. Several limitations are worth noting:

They assume equilibrium. Real corrosion is a kinetic process. A metal may be thermodynamically unstable but corrode very slowly because the oxide film is protective (passivation). Aluminium in neutral water is a good example: the Pourbaix diagram says it should dissolve, but the Al₂O₃ film prevents it.

They are usually drawn for pure metals in pure water at 25°C and standard concentrations ($10^{-6}$ M dissolved species by convention). Real environments contain chlorides, sulphates, dissolved oxygen, biological organisms, and other complications.
They do not show kinetic information: corrosion rates, pitting susceptibility, or stress corrosion cracking.
Temperature effects are significant. A Pourbaix diagram at 25°C may not be relevant for a boiler operating at 250°C.

Despite these limitations, Pourbaix diagrams are enormously useful as a first screening tool. They tell you whether corrosion is thermodynamically possible, what form it might take (active dissolution vs. passivation), and what conditions (potential, pH) might prevent it. The kinetic details come from experiments and more detailed models, but the Pourbaix diagram tells you where to look.

Every boundary on a predominance diagram comes from a single equilibrium calculation: set $\Delta G = 0$ for the reaction between two adjacent phases and solve for the relationship between the axis variables. For a Pourbaix diagram, this means applying the Nernst equation:
where $n$ is the number of electrons transferred, $F = 96485$ C/mol is Faraday's constant, and $Q$ is the reaction quotient. At 25°C, $RT/F = 0.02569$ V.

For more complex systems (ternary alloys, multiple gas species, high temperatures), the calculations become involved but the principle is the same. Software tools (FactSage, HSC Chemistry, Thermo-Calc) automate the construction of predominance diagrams for arbitrary systems using the same free energy databases that underlie CALPHAD phase diagrams. The thermodynamic framework is identical; only the choice of axes differs.

On the Pourbaix diagram for iron at 25°C, the Fe/Fe$^{2+}$ boundary is at approximately $E = -0.62$ V (vs SHE), independent of pH. Explain why this boundary is horizontal, and calculate the equilibrium concentration of Fe$^{2+}$ if the potential is $-0.44$ V (the standard electrode potential for Fe).
The reaction Fe $\to$ Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$ involves no H$^+$ or OH$^-$, so the equilibrium potential does not depend on pH. The boundary is horizontal.
The boundary is drawn at $[\text{Fe}^{2+}] = 10^{-6}$ M (the conventional threshold for "significant corrosion"):
This matches the $-0.62$ V boundary on the diagram. At $E = -0.44$ V (the standard potential), $[\text{Fe}^{2+}] = 1$ M: the iron is actively corroding and dissolving at a high rate.
